extra.message: Hardcoded default Django SECRET_KEY fallback enables session forgery — Session hijacking, CSRF bypass, password reset token forgery, arbitrary code execution via signed cookie deserialization. [verified: settings.py line 17 defines SECRET_KEY with a hardcoded default fallback 'dev-only-change-me-hr-payroll-portal-not-for-production' when DJANGO_SECRET_KEY env var is unset; this known secret enables forgery of sessions, CSRF tokens, and password reset tokens in any deployment that omits the env var.]

Hardcoded Default Django SECRET_KEY — Session hijacking, CSRF token forgery, account takeover via password reset token forgery. [verified: Same hardcoded default SECRET_KEY at settings.py line 17 as finding [0]; if DJANGO_SECRET_KEY is not set at deployment, all cryptographic signing becomes trivially forgeable by anyone who knows the default string.]

DEBUG mode enabled by default — Detailed error pages expose stack traces, database queries, settings (including SECRET_KEY), and local variables to unauthenticated users, facilitating targeted attacks. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default at settings.py line 18 as findings [1] and [3]; Django debug error pages expose stack traces, database queries, settings including SECRET_KEY, and local variables to unauthenticated users when deployed without explicitly setting DJANGO_DEBUG=false.]

DEBUG Mode Enabled by Default — Information disclosure via detailed error pages, exposure of internal paths and variables, potentially interactive debugger access. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default at settings.py line 18 as finding [1]; detailed error pages with local variables and paths are exposed if DJANGO_DEBUG is not explicitly set to a falsy value in production.]

No rate limiting on login endpoint enables password brute-force — Automated password guessing / credential stuffing against all user accounts via the login page. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware (django-axes, django-ratelimit, or custom) exists anywhere in the codebase; Django's built-in auth login at /accounts/login/ has no brute-force throttling, lockout, or attempt tracking.]

TLS certificate verification disabled for outbound HTTPS connections — Man-in-the-middle attacks on outbound HTTPS connections, enabling interception and tampering of payroll data sent to external partners. [verified: payroll_trust_drift_647 explicitly uses ssl._create_unverified_context() to disable TLS certificate verification on outbound HTTPS; the threat model lists 'HTTPS requests with disabled verification' as a trust boundary concern, and though the hardcoded domain is partner.invalid, the missing control is genuinely present on a reachable path gated only by the internal token.]

Business Logic Bypass: Employees can self-resolve or close their own HR requests — Employees can unilaterally close or mark as resolved their HR requests, circumventing organizational controls and HR oversight. [verified: can_change_hr_request returns True for employees on their own OPEN/WAITING_ON_EMPLOYEE requests (owns_employee check at services.py:223), yet request_status allows setting any valid status including resolved/closed without restricting employee-eligible targets; the template also shows all four status buttons unconditionally.]

CSV Formula Injection in Data Exports — Code execution on the machine of anyone opening the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application with default settings. [verified: Same CSV formula-injection sink in the same three export views as finding 0 — no sanitization exists on any of the exported columns (employee names, department codes, task titles, policy titles).]

CSV Formula Injection in spreadsheet exports — When exported CSVs are opened in spreadsheet applications, malicious formulas execute DDE commands, exfiltrate data from the viewer's machine, or run arbitrary commands. [verified: Same unguarded csv.writer output of user-controlled fields (employee_id, full_name, department code, task title, policy title) as findings 0 and 1 — identical lack of formula-prefix stripping or spreadsheet-safe encoding across all three export endpoints.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Account takeover via brute-force password guessing, credential stuffing, or invite token enumeration. [verified: No rate-limiting mechanism (django-axes, django-defender, or custom middleware) exists in requirements.txt or the MIDDLEWARE list; authentication endpoints /accounts/login/, /accounts/password_reset/, and /invite/<token>/ are reachable without any throttling, enabling brute-force attacks against user credentials and invite tokens.]

Session cookies transmitted without Secure flag — Session hijacking via network sniffing, leading to full account takeover and access to sensitive payroll/HR data. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is never set in settings.py (Django defaults to False), and no compensating HTTPS enforcement (SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS, or SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER) exists anywhere in the codebase — cookies are transmitted over plain HTTP.]
